summary.text: From time 1 onward, the zero cells are identified with the odd entries of a spatially shifted Pascal triangle modulo 2: Pascal’s identity and Rule 167 both propagate them by XOR, and the relevant central binomial coefficient is odd exactly when the time is a power of 2. This is also exactly when \(n\mid 2^{n+1}\), so appending the next middle-column bit to the binary prefix—doubling and adding that bit—gives the claimed recurrence.

full_proof.text:
Let \(C(t,x)\in\{0,1\}\) denote the state at time \(t\geq 0\) and position \(x\in\mathbb Z\) of the Rule 167 cellular automaton begun from the single black cell
\[
C(0,x)=\begin{cases}1,&x=0,\\0,&x\ne0.\end{cases}
\]
For three input bits \(L,C,R\), Rule 167 returns the bit in position \(4L+2C+R\) of the binary expansion of \(167\). Thus its truth table is
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
(L,C,R)&\text{output}\\ \hline
000&1\\
001&1\\
010&1\\
011&0\\
100&0\\
101&1\\
110&0\\
111&1.
\end{array}
\]
The update convention is
\[
C(t+1,x)=\operatorname{Rule}_{167}\bigl(C(t,x-1),C(t,x),C(t,x+1)\bigr).
\]
Write
\[
b_t=C(t,0)
\]
for the middle-column bit. The sequence in question is the value of the binary prefix \(b_0b_1\cdots b_n\), namely
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}b_k2^{n-k}.
\]
We prove that, for every \(n\geq2\),
\[
a(n)=2a(n-1)+1-\left\lfloor(1/2)^{\,2^{n+1}\bmod n}\right\rfloor.
\]

The main point is to characterize exactly when the middle-column bit is zero.

Define, for \(t\geq1\), a predicate \(Z(t,x)\) by
\[
Z(t,x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{there is a }j\in\{0,1,\ldots,t-1\}\text{ such that }
 x=2-t+2j
\text{ and }\binom{t-1}{j}\text{ is odd}.
\]
We will show that
\[
C(t,x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Z(t,x)                       \tag{1}
\]
for every \(t\geq1\) and every integer \(x\). In fact, all cells not satisfying \(Z(t,x)\) have value \(1\).

First observe that two positions satisfying \(Z(t,\cdot)\) can never be adjacent. Indeed, every such position has the form \(2-t+2j\), so the difference between any two such positions is even. In particular,
\[
Z(t,x)\Longrightarrow \neg Z(t,x+1),\qquad
Z(t,x)\Longrightarrow \neg Z(t,x-1).                       \tag{2}
\]

We next record how the truth table simplifies under this nonadjacency condition. Suppose three input bits are written in the form
\[
L=\begin{cases}0,&P,\\1,&\neg P,\end{cases}\quad
C=\begin{cases}0,&Q,\\1,&\neg Q,\end{cases}\quad
R=\begin{cases}0,&R_0,\\1,&\neg R_0,\end{cases}
\]
where \(P\) means that the left input is zero, \(Q\) that the center input is zero, and \(R_0\) that the right input is zero. Assume that a zero left input and a zero center input cannot occur together, and likewise that a zero right input and a zero center input cannot occur together. Inspection of the eight entries in the Rule 167 table then gives
\[
\operatorname{Rule}_{167}(L,C,R)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(P\wedge\neg R_0)\ \vee\ (\neg P\wedge R_0).                \tag{3}
\]
Thus, among configurations in which the center zero is not adjacent to another zero, the new cell is zero precisely when exactly one of the two outer inputs is zero.

Now we show that the sets \(Z(t,\cdot)\) satisfy exactly this same recursion. For every \(t\geq1\),
\[
Z(t+1,x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\bigl(Z(t,x-1)\wedge\neg Z(t,x+1)\bigr)
\vee
\bigl(\neg Z(t,x-1)\wedge Z(t,x+1)\bigr).                  \tag{4}
\]
To see this, suppose first that \(x\) is in the support allowed at time \(t+1\), so
\[
x=2-(t+1)+2j=1-t+2j,
\qquad 0\leq j\leq t.
\]
The two outer positions in the preceding row are
\[
x-1=-t+2j=2-t+2(j-1),
\qquad
x+1=2-t+2j.
\]
Consequently, when \(1\leq j\leq t-1\), the condition \(Z(t,x-1)\) is exactly the oddness of \(\binom{t-1}{j-1}\), while \(Z(t,x+1)\) is exactly the oddness of \(\binom{t-1}{j}\). Pascal's identity says
\[
\binom tj=\binom{t-1}{j-1}+\binom{t-1}{j}.
\]
A sum of two integers is odd precisely when exactly one summand is odd. Hence \(\binom tj\) is odd precisely when exactly one of the two preceding conditions holds.

The two boundary cases give the same conclusion. If \(j=0\), then the right predecessor has index \(0\) and coefficient \(\binom{t-1}{0}=1\), while there is no left predecessor in the allowed support; hence exactly the right predecessor lies in \(Z\). If \(j=t\), then the left predecessor has index \(t-1\) and coefficient \(\binom{t-1}{t-1}=1\), while there is no right predecessor in the allowed support. Conversely, if one of \(x-1,x+1\) lies in the preceding support, its coordinate uniquely determines the corresponding index \(j-1\) or \(j\), and the same Pascal identity, including these endpoint cases, reconstructs an odd \(\binom tj\). This proves (4).

We can now prove (1) by induction on \(t\). At time \(1\), direct use of the initial condition gives the neighborhoods
\[
001\text{ at }x=-1,\qquad010\text{ at }x=0,\qquad100\text{ at }x=1,
\]
and \(000\) at every other position. Rule 167 sends only the neighborhood \(100\) among these to zero. Therefore
\[
C(1,x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=1.
\]
On the other hand, the definition of \(Z(1,x)\) permits only \(j=0\), and gives
\[
x=2-1+0=1,
\qquad \binom00=1,
\]
so (1) holds at time \(1\).

Assume it holds at time \(t\geq1\). Then the three inputs at position \(x\) and time \(t+1\) are zero exactly when, respectively,
\[
Z(t,x-1),\qquad Z(t,x),\qquad Z(t,x+1)
\]
hold. By (2), the middle condition cannot occur together with either outer condition. Therefore the truth-table reduction (3) applies, showing that the new output is zero exactly when precisely one of \(Z(t,x-1)\) and \(Z(t,x+1)\) holds. By (4), this is exactly \(Z(t+1,x)\). This completes the induction and proves (1).

We next specialize (1) to the center \(x=0\). If \(Z(n,0)\) holds, then for some \(j\),
\[
0=2-n+2j,
\]
so
\[
n=2(j+1).
\]
Put \(m=j+1\). The relevant coefficient then becomes
\[
\binom{n-1}{j}=\binom{2m-1}{m-1}.                         \tag{5}
\]
Thus the classification of center zeroes reduces to the following binomial parity fact:
\[
\binom{2m-1}{m-1}\text{ is odd}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
m\text{ is a power of }2.                                  \tag{6}
\]
We now prove (6).

We use the elementary mod-2 digit reduction
\[
\binom NK\equiv
\binom{N\bmod2}{K\bmod2}
\binom{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}{\lfloor K/2\rfloor}
\pmod2.                                                     \tag{7}
\]
For completeness, this follows by comparing coefficients over the field with two elements. Write \(N=2q+\varepsilon\), with \(\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}\). In characteristic two,
\[
(1+X)^N=(1+X)^\varepsilon\bigl((1+X)^2\bigr)^q
=(1+X)^\varepsilon(1+X^2)^q.
\]
The coefficient of \(X^{2s+\delta}\), \(\delta\in\{0,1\}\), is therefore
\(\binom\varepsilon\delta\binom qs\), which is (7).

We prove (6) by strong induction on \(m\geq1\). For \(m=1\), the coefficient is \(\binom10=1\), and \(1=2^0\).

Suppose first that \(m\) is even, say \(m=2r\), where \(r\geq1\). Then (7), applied to \(N=4r-1\) and \(K=2r-1\), gives
\[
\binom{4r-1}{2r-1}
\equiv
\binom11\binom{2r-1}{r-1}
\equiv \binom{2r-1}{r-1}\pmod2.                            \tag{8}
\]
By the induction hypothesis, the last coefficient is odd exactly when \(r\) is a power of two. This is equivalent to \(2r=m\) being a power of two: if \(r=2^k\), then \(m=2^{k+1}\); conversely, if \(2r=2^k\), then \(k\neq0\) and \(r=2^{k-1}\).

Suppose instead that \(m>1\) is odd. Write \(m=2r+1\), where necessarily \(r\geq1\). Formula (7), now with \(N=4r+1\) and \(K=2r\), gives
\[
\binom{4r+1}{2r}
\equiv
\binom10\binom{2r}{r}
\equiv\binom{2r}{r}\pmod2.                                 \tag{9}
\]
The central binomial coefficient on the right is even. Indeed, Pascal's identity and symmetry give
\[
\binom{2r}{r}
= inom{2r-1}{r-1}+\binom{2r-1}{r}
=2\binom{2r-1}{r-1}.
\]
Thus the coefficient in (9) is even. At the same time, an odd integer greater than \(1\) cannot be a power of two. Hence both sides of (6) are false in this case. This completes the strong induction and proves (6).

We can now classify the center. For \(n\geq2\),
\[
Z(n,0)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\text{ is a power of }2.       \tag{10}
\]
Indeed, if \(Z(n,0)\), the coordinate equation gives \(n=2m\), and (5) is odd; by (6), \(m=2^k\), so \(n=2^{k+1}\). Conversely, if \(n=2^q\) and \(n\geq2\), then \(q\geq1\). Set
\[
m=2^{q-1},\qquad j=m-1.
\]
Then \(0=2-n+2j\), the index satisfies \(0\leq j\leq n-1\), and by (6),
\[
\binom{n-1}{j}=\binom{2m-1}{m-1}
\]
is odd. Hence \(Z(n,0)\).

Combining (1) and (10), we obtain the exact middle-column bit:
\[
b_n=C(n,0)=
\begin{cases}
0,&n\text{ is a power of }2,\\
1,&n\text{ is not a power of }2,
\end{cases}
\qquad(n\geq2).                                             \tag{11}
\]

It remains to identify the floor term with the complementary indicator. Let
\[
r_n=2^{n+1}\bmod n.
\]
Since \(r_n\) is a nonnegative integer,
\[
\left\lfloor(1/2)^{r_n}\right\rfloor
=\begin{cases}1,&r_n=0,\\0,&r_n>0.\end{cases}               \tag{12}
\]
Moreover, for \(n\geq2\),
\[
r_n=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\mid2^{n+1}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\text{ is a power of }2.                                  \tag{13}
\]
The first equivalence is the definition of remainder. For the second, if \(n\mid2^{n+1}\), every prime divisor of \(n\) must divide \(2^{n+1}\), and hence must be \(2\); unique prime factorization then gives \(n=2^k\) for some \(k\). Conversely, if \(n=2^k\), then \(k\leq2^k+1=n+1\), so \(2^k\mid2^{n+1}\). Therefore, if we denote the floor term by \(F(n)\), (12) and (13) say
\[
F(n)=\left\lfloor(1/2)^{\,2^{n+1}\bmod n}\right\rfloor
=\begin{cases}
1,&n\text{ is a power of }2,\\
0,&n\text{ is not a power of }2.
\end{cases}                                                  \tag{14}
\]
Comparison of (11) and (14) gives, for every \(n\geq2\),
\[
b_n=1-F(n).                                                 \tag{15}
\]

Finally, the definition of a binary prefix immediately yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{n}b_k2^{n-k}\\
&=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}b_k2^{n-k}+b_n\\
&=2\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}b_k2^{(n-1)-k}+b_n\\
&=2a(n-1)+b_n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Using (15), we conclude that for every integer \(n\geq2\),
\[
\boxed{
a(n)=2a(n-1)+1-
\left\lfloor(1/2)^{(2^{n+1}\bmod n)}\right\rfloor
}.
\]
This is the claimed recurrence.
